searchText: 🤔 out loud... I wonder how much value an Ethereum turn style has for monetary policy? I was trolling through various accounts on Ethereum today and there is a *lot* of ETH that show signs of being "lost" or "permanently stuck". The big disadvantage of a turn style is that it is directly counter to long term cold storage. I do wonder though if a turn style every 5 or 10 years would be worth it, or if it just introduces too much risk making everyone have to touch their ETH once every 5 or 10 years? I think that if unmoved Ether is considered lost it should be done so at a policy level _i.e._ if someone wants to say "any Ether unmoved for 5 years is lost" they're welcome to do so, and to publish their total supply accordingly, but the chain itself shouldn't ever assume. (It also avoids the whole "well if you're mucking about with chain balances then please can you..." requests) Who is "they" in this? I wasn't thinking about mucking about with balances, just make it so fees are paid with ETH-B instead of ETH-A as of some block, and anyone can convert ETH-A to ETH-B anytime before that block. (where that block is sufficiently in the future) I suppose it would be simpler and cheaper to just say that any account that hasn't been touched for `n` years is unusable. Whomsoever is publishing total supply numbers, or bases their economic analysis of the soundness of Ethereum on some sort of current and/or future value of total supply. It feels to me that removing "stale" balances is something that doesn't really fit for Ethereum. You could apply the same argument to removing "stale" state, for example, but in both cases there is an argument that reading the information is as important, if not more so, than writing the information and as we can't track who reads what we can't ever say that anything is unused. Oh, the idea is that it must be enforced. From an economic standpoint (thinking of ETH like "money"), I think there is value in understanding just how scarce it is. From the standpoint of "ETH is just the fee token", there is no need as you either have tokens to pay for fees or you don't. Whether that economic value is worth the costs associated with getting an accurate number (e.g., turn style) I'm very much uncertain of, and I lean toward "not worth it" at the moment. Although true, I do think that direction of travel is more important for long-term analysis. If total supply is increasing at x%, or decreasing at y%, that seems to be a more useful metric than current total supply. The % change is derived from total supply, so we cannot know the % change without knowing the total supply. I'd worry about how many people you manage to annoy (or, indeed, make significantly poorer) as a result of doing it. Yeah, certainly. And there are risks to asking people to pull their keys out of cold storage. Every time that happens there is a chance of someone screwing something up. True, sorry my point was badly worded. And my brain doesn't seem to be up to rephrasing in a way that makes it any clearer. But I think we're in broad agreement anyway that it's a risk/reward thing where the risk seems high. How much genesis eth is unmoved?
